chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn from Ali ibn Asbat from al-Husayn ibn Abi al-'Ala' from Sa'd al-Iskaf who said:

A man came to the Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) asking him about the Spirit, 'Is it not Jibra'il?'. So the Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) said to him: 'Jibra'il (peace be upon him) is from the Angels, and the Spirit is other than Jibra'il'. He reiterated that upon the man, so he said to him: 'You have spoken a great thing from the speech. There is no one claiming that the Spirit is other than Jibra'il'.
So the Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) said to him: 'You have strayed and are reporting from the strayed people'.

Allah the Exalted is Saying to His Prophet (peace be upon him and his family): 'Allah's Command will come, therefore do not hasten it; Glory be to Him, and Exalted is He above what they are describing. He Sends down the Angels with the Spirit, and the Spirit is other than the Angels'.
May the Salawat of Allah be upon them.
ai.seo_question: What is the difference between Jibra'il and the Spirit in Shia theology?
ai.summary: In this narration from *Al-Kafi*, Imam Ali (AS) distinguishes 'Al-Ruh' from Jibra'il by citing the verse 'He sends down the Angels with the Spirit,' indicating that while Jibra'il is an angel, the Spirit is a distinct, higher ontological reality often associated with the divine command or the soul. This distinction is crucial in Shia theology for understanding the nature of revelation and the spiritual sustenance of the Imams, separating the messenger (angel) from the essential life-force or divine decree (spirit). The hadith serves as a refutation of those who conflate the two, emphasizing the transcendence of the Spirit beyond the category of mere angels.
